sections.section_title: The Promise That Remains and the Danger of Falling Short
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds the author warns that since the promise of entering God's rest remains open and the wilderness generation forfeited their access through unbelief, the audience must fear lest any among them fall short -- noting that the wilderness generation also had good news preached to them, but the word did not benefit them because it was not united with faith.
sections.relevance: The passage directly addresses the believer's standing by warning that hearing the good news is insufficient without ongoing faith. The author's call to 'fear' (phobēthōmen, first person plural) is directed at the community of faith. The perfect infinitive 'have come short' (hysterekentai) suggests the author fears some may already be in this condition. The parallel between the two communities is exact: 'we have had good news preached to us, just as they also did.' The critical difference is whether the word is 'united with faith' (synkekerasmenous tē pistei) in the hearers. The implication is that hearing the gospel, even genuinely, does not automatically guarantee entry into the rest -- faith must be fused with the word for it to benefit the hearer.
key_phrases: let us fear
any one of you may seem to have come short
the word they heard did not benefit them
not united with those who listened with faith

sections.section_title: The Rest That Has Existed Since Creation
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds the author argues that God's rest has existed since the foundation of the world (citing Genesis 2:2) and that the oath excluding the disobedient from this rest (Psalm 95:11) presupposes a rest that predates and outlasts any generation's failure to enter it.
sections.relevance: The section establishes that 'we who have believed enter that rest' -- making faith the condition of entry -- while simultaneously re-citing the oath excluding the unbelieving. The juxtaposition of positive entry through belief and negative exclusion through unbelief reinforces the conditionality of access to God's rest. The rest itself is permanent (it has existed since creation), but participation in it depends on faith.
key_phrases: we who have believed enter that rest
They certainly shall not enter My rest
His works were finished from the foundation of the world

sections.section_title: The Argument from Today -- David's Witness
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds the author argues that since the rest remains open and the previous recipients failed through disobedience, God designated a new 'Today' through David centuries later, proving the promise was not exhausted by the wilderness generation's failure or Joshua's conquest.
sections.relevance: The section reinforces conditionality by establishing that 'those who previously had good news preached to them failed to enter because of disobedience' (apeitheian), and that God's reopening of the offer through David's 'Today' means the same choice confronts each generation. The equation of unbelief (3:19) with disobedience (4:6) confirms the author treats them as inseparable: to refuse to trust God's word is to disobey it.
key_phrases: those who previously had good news preached to them failed to enter because of disobedience
Today if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts

sections.section_title: Joshua Did Not Give the Rest
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds the author uses a counterfactual argument to show that Joshua's settlement of Israel in the land did not constitute the ultimate rest God promised, since David's psalm, written centuries later, still speaks of entering God's rest as an open possibility.

The neutral reading finds the author concludes that a sabbatismos (Sabbath rest) remains for the people of God -- a participation in God's own completed work, modeled on the seventh-day rest of creation, distinct from any territorial or temporal rest.

The neutral reading finds this verse commands strenuous effort to enter the rest, with the explicit warning that the wilderness generation's disobedience serves as a pattern that can be replicated: 'so that no one will fall by following the same example of disobedience.'
sections.relevance: The passage directly addresses the believer's standing by presenting entry into God's rest as requiring sustained, active, persistent faith -- not passive reception. The verb spoudazō ('make every effort') demands diligence. The word 'fall' (pesē) echoes the fate of the wilderness generation whose corpses 'fell' in the wilderness (3:17). The word 'example' (hypodeigma) treats the wilderness failure not as an unrepeatable event but as a type that the audience can replicate. The author's argument throughout chapters 3-4 has consistently treated the audience's situation as parallel to the wilderness generation's: both received the good news, both face the same choice, and both risk the same outcome if they fail to believe and obey.
key_phrases: let us make every effort to enter that rest
so that no one will fall
the same example of disobedience

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds the author describes the word of God as living, active, and penetrating -- able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart -- and asserts that no creature is hidden from God's sight, all things being laid bare before the one to whom we must give account.
sections.relevance: The passage functions as the theological warrant for the preceding warnings: the audience cannot hear God's word and remain unmoved, nor can they conceal an unbelieving heart behind outward participation. The word of God forces a choice -- one either softens and believes or hardens and resists. The transition from the judging word to the all-seeing God ('Him to whom we must answer') establishes that the community's internal spiritual state is fully known to God. This closes off the possibility of casual, consequence-free hearing and reinforces the urgency of genuine faith rather than mere external association with the community.
key_phrases: the word of God is living and active
sharper than any two-edged sword
able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart
all things are open and laid bare to the eyes of Him to whom we must answer

sections.section_title: The Great High Priest -- Transition and Assurance
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this section pivots from warning to encouragement: because the audience has a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and who sympathizes with their weaknesses (having been tempted in all things without sin), they are called to hold firmly to their confession and to approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and timely help.
sections.relevance: The passage contains both assurance and conditionality. The assurance is substantial: Jesus sympathizes, the throne dispenses grace, mercy and help are available in the time of need. But the passage frames these resources as requiring active response: 'let us hold firmly to our confession' (kratōmen, a strong verb meaning to grasp and refuse to let go) and 'let us approach' (proserchōmetha). The imperative to 'hold firmly' implies that the confession can be released -- consistent with the same verb and concept in 3:6 and 3:14. The overall movement of 4:1-16 traces an arc from 'let us fear' to 'let us approach with confidence,' holding both danger and resource simultaneously without dissolving either.
key_phrases: let us hold firmly to our confession
tempted in all things just as we are, yet without sin
let us approach the throne of grace with confidence
mercy and find grace for help at the time of our need
